---
title: "Why ten thousand steps"
description: "The number came from a Japanese pedometer marketing campaign in 1965. It is still the number, because round numbers become goals whether they deserve to or not."
author: "Mesfin Genie"
date: "2026-09-12"
categories: [behavioural economics, everyday]
---

Ten thousand steps a day. You have probably tried to hit it. Your phone may be
counting right now.

The figure has no clinical origin. It came from a pedometer sold in Japan in
1965, named with a character that looks like a walking person and translates
roughly as "ten thousand steps meter". It was a product name. It stuck because
it is round.

We are drawn to round numbers as targets in a way that has nothing to do with
evidence. Marathon finishers cluster just under four hours, not because bodies
change at 3:59 but because people push for the number. Savings goals are
$10,000 rather than $9,300. Diets target 1,500 calories, not 1,437. The
roundness gives the goal a shape, and a shape is easier to want.

It cuts both ways. A round target can pull real effort out of you; the
runners at 3:59 did run faster. It can also be arbitrary in ways that cost
you. Research on step counts suggests most of the benefit arrives well before
10,000, and that for many older adults the curve flattens closer to 7,000.
Someone who does 7,500 and feels like a failure has been misled by a number
that was invented to sell a gadget.

If a round number gets you moving, keep it. Just know where it came from, and
do not let it tell you that 8,000 is nothing.
